transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, um... I guess I'm here because I just... I really can’t shake this feeling, this just constant, heavy feeling that I’ve completely ruined things for everyone. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like this weight that follows me around all day. 

It really started getting bad with work. I do computer support, you know, IT stuff, so people really depend on me to keep their systems running and fix their issues so they can do their own jobs. But lately, I’ve just been falling so far behind. The tickets just pile up in the queue, and I just sit there knowing my coworkers are having to pick up my slack, and I’m just letting the whole team down. 

And then, because of all that, I come home and... well, I’ve just completely lost control of the apartment situation. It’s a total disaster. Just things piling up there too, and I can't seem to manage the most basic upkeep to keep the place together. I just look around at the apartment, and I think about the mess I'm making at work, and I just feel so incredibly guilty. Like I'm just dragging everyone down with me. Honestly, it's gotten to the point where I feel like I deserve whatever bad thing happens next. If things just fall apart completely... I feel like I brought it on myself and I deserve it, you know? I just can't stop thinking that way, and I didn't know what else to do but come in.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

No, honestly... no, not at all. It’s actually really frustrating because... well, most days I wake up with this just... this flat, heavy sadness. Right from the second I open my eyes, it's just sitting there. And I used to have these things, these activities that would sort of reset me, you know? Like a palate cleanser for my brain after a long week of dealing with frustrated users and broken servers. 

I’ve got this pretty extensive vinyl collection—mostly vintage jazz and some 70s prog rock—and I used to love just picking out a record, cleaning the dust off, dropping the needle, and really actively listening to it. Or cooking. I used to spend my whole Sunday afternoon making a proper ragu from scratch, letting it simmer for hours, chopping all the fresh herbs... or tinkering with electronics. That was a really big one for me. I have this little workbench setup in the apartment where I build custom mechanical keyboards and mess around with microcontrollers. I used to get so absorbed in soldering the little components, getting the switches just right, testing the circuits. It was so satisfying to fix something and see it work. 

But lately... I don't know, none of it reaches me anymore. I try, I really do. I’ll sit at the workbench and look at the circuit boards, or I'll stare at my record shelves, and it’s just... nothing. It just feels like a massive chore. The music just sounds like background noise now, so I don't even bother turning the amplifier on. And the thought of cooking just completely exhausts me, so I just eat whatever is in a wrapper. That heavy sadness just kind of blankets all of it, and the things that used to make me feel like myself, the things that used to bring me back to baseline... they just don't work anymore. I just end up sitting there, feeling exactly as flat and empty as I did when I woke up.
Have you had thoughts of harming yourself?

Well, um... no, I don't have a plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting here figuring out how to, you know, actually do something to myself. But... I mean, if I'm being completely honest, and I guess that's why I'm here, right? To be honest about all this... I do catch myself having these thoughts. A lot, actually. 

It's usually when I'm lying in bed at night, looking up at the ceiling, just dreading the next day. Dreading having to face the ticket queue, dreading having to see my coworkers and know they're carrying my weight. And I just think... I think it would just be so much easier if I just didn't wake up. Like, if my heart just stopped in my sleep or something. It wouldn't be me doing it, it would just happen. And then... well, then it would just be over. The guilt, the heavy feeling, the mess in the apartment. All of it. 

And more than that, I think about how it would be easier for everyone else, too. Because right now, I feel like this massive burden. I feel like I'm just this anchor dragging my team down, dragging everyone around me down. And if I just wasn't here... if I just quietly slipped away in my sleep... then nobody would have to deal with me anymore. They could hire someone who actually does the job right, who doesn't let the tickets pile up. My landlord could clear out the apartment and rent it to someone who actually cleans. It just... it feels like the math works out better if I'm just not in the equation, you know? But no, I wouldn't do it myself. I don't have a plan to hurt myself. It's just this constant, lingering wish that I could just... disappear.
How long have you been feeling this heavy sadness and guilt?

Well, um... let me think. It’s been a while now. I’d say... yeah, it’s been about a year and two months. I remember exactly when it started, actually, because it was right around the time I had to move. 

See, I used to live in this great place over on 4th Street. It had this big window where the afternoon light would come in right onto my workbench, which was perfect for soldering because you really need good light for that, you know? But then, in the middle of winter, a pipe burst in the unit above mine. It was a complete disaster. Water came pouring through the ceiling, ruined a bunch of my vintage jazz records—I lost an original pressing of 'Kind of Blue' that I had hunted down at a flea market, which just broke my heart. 

Anyway, the building management had to do all this remediation, pulling out drywall and everything, so they moved me into a different unit on the ground floor. But it’s so much smaller, and it’s dark, and I couldn't set up my workbench the same way. I couldn't organize my records. My whole routine just completely fell apart. I couldn't come home and unwind the way I used to. And that’s when it started, really. That’s when the heavy feeling just sort of moved in with me into that new apartment. I thought it was just the stress of the move at first, you know? Dealing with the insurance and the damaged stuff and trying to figure out where to put my keyboard parts in a place with half the closet space. But the boxes just stayed packed, and the feeling never left. It just kept getting heavier and heavier, and spreading into my work, and now here we are, a year and two months later, and I just... I can't shake it.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or how quickly you move and react to things?

Well, yeah, actually. It's... it's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to get through the ticket queue. It's like... you know when you're trying to use a remote desktop connection to fix a user's machine, and their internet is just terrible, so there's this massive lag between when you click the mouse and when the cursor actually moves on their screen? That's exactly how my body feels right now. 

Like, at work, I'll be sitting there, and I know exactly what I need to type to resolve a simple password reset or a printer mapping issue—stuff I've done a thousand times, stuff I could usually do in my sleep. But my hands will just... hover over the keyboard. I'll just sit there staring at the keys, and it's like the signal from my brain is just taking forever to reach my fingers. It takes me so much longer to answer even the most basic support tickets now. 

And it's not just typing, it's everything. Getting out of a chair feels like I'm moving underwater. Even just turning my head when someone calls my name from the next cubicle... I know I'm reacting slowly, I can feel it happening, but I can't speed it up. It's like my brain and my body are running on this awful, delayed connection, and the latency is just getting worse and worse. I used to be the guy who could juggle three chat windows and a phone call all at once, typing ninety words a minute, and now... now I'm just staring at my hands, waiting for them to do what I'm telling them to do. It's exhausting, honestly. Just the physical act of moving through the day feels like it takes twice the energy it used to.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight? Um... well, no, not really. I mean, I guess I haven't really been paying that much attention to it, to be honest. It's not like I have a scale in my apartment or anything. I used to have one, actually, back at the old place on 4th Street, this nice digital one with the glass top, but it got smashed when they were moving my stuff out after the pipe burst. The movers just tossed it in a box with some heavy books, and that was the end of that. 

But anyway, no, my clothes seem to fit about the same as they always have. I mean, my routine is pretty much identical every day, so I guess my eating habits haven't really shifted. I still just grab a bagel from the cart outside my building on the way to the subway, and then usually just order whatever the rest of the team is getting for lunch—usually Thai or pizza, something easy we can eat at our desks while we try to burn down the ticket queue. And then for dinner, well, I usually just microwave something when I get home, if I have the energy, or just make a sandwich. So, yeah, I'm pretty sure I'm still hovering right around the same weight I've been for the last few years. I haven't noticed my belt getting any looser or tighter, or anything like that. It's just... everything else feels so heavy, you know? But physically, no, my weight hasn't changed.
Have you ever thought about how you would disappear or make it happen if you weren't here anymore?

Well, um... no, I haven't really thought about *how* I would do anything like that. I mean, I don't have a plan to hurt myself or anything. It's not like I'm sitting there figuring out logistics or researching methods or whatever. I don't want to actively do something to end it. But... I do catch myself thinking about it in a different way. 

It’s more like... well, you know how sometimes you have a really awful day at work, where the servers keep crashing, and the phone won't stop ringing, and users are yelling at you because they forgot their own passwords, and you just get home and you're so utterly drained that you just collapse onto the bed and you think, "I just want to sleep for a week"? It's kind of like that, but... deeper. And darker, I guess. 

I just catch myself thinking that it would be so much easier if I just went to sleep and didn't wake up. Like, if my system just naturally powered down and didn't reboot. Because right now, every day is just this massive effort, dragging myself through the motions, feeling this weight, dealing with the lag in my own body. And then there's the guilt, feeling like I'm letting my team down because my ticket resolution time has tanked, and I'm just a burden to everyone around me. If I just wasn't here... if I just faded out in my sleep... then nobody would have to deal with me anymore. The team could hire someone who actually has the energy to do the job right, and my landlord could rent this dark little ground-floor apartment to someone who doesn't mind it, and I wouldn't have to feel this... this crushing heaviness every single second of the day. So, yeah, no plans, no intent to make it happen myself. Just... a really strong wish for an automatic shutdown, I guess.
Have you experienced any strange or unusual thoughts, like hearing voices or seeing things that others can't?

Well, um... yeah, actually. It's... it's kind of hard to talk about because I know how it sounds, and working in IT, you know, I'm used to things having a logical explanation, a root cause that you can trace back and fix. But lately, especially since I moved into this smaller apartment after the pipe burst at the old place... some nights, it gets really weird. 

It usually happens when it's super quiet, like after 2:00 AM, when the street noise dies down and I'm just lying there trying to sleep, staring at the ceiling. I'll start hearing this... this dripping sound. Like water hitting a puddle. And at first, I thought, "Great, another plumbing issue," because of what happened at the last place, you know? So I'd get up and check the kitchen sink, the bathroom, the radiator, everywhere. But it's bone dry. And the dripping doesn't sound like it's coming from the pipes anyway. It sounds like it's coming from the corner of the living room, right where I have all my old vinyl records boxed up. I haven't unpacked them because there's just no space here, and honestly, I haven't had the energy to set up the turntable anyway. 

But it's not just the dripping. That's the thing. Sometimes... sometimes mixed in with that dripping sound, I'll hear a voice. A really low, muffled voice, kind of like it's coming through a wall or a bad headset connection. And it's saying my name. Just... my name, over and over, really slowly. The first time it happened, I actually walked over to the boxes and stood there in the dark, just listening, trying to figure out if it was a neighbor or someone outside the window, because this place is on the ground floor. But the sound was coming from *inside* the room. From the boxes. And it sounds so incredibly real. I mean, I know it can't be real—there's nobody there, there's no water, it's just cardboard and old records—but in that moment, it sounds as clear as you and me talking right now. It really freaks me out, to be honest. I end up just putting my noise-canceling headphones on and playing white noise until the sun comes up, because I just can't deal with it.
Do you believe the voice you hear is real?

Well, um... that's... that's the thing that really messes with my head, honestly. Because, like I said, I work in IT. My entire job, my whole career, is based on logic. If a server is down, there's a reason. If a script fails, there's a syntax error or a permission issue. There's always a root cause. So, the logical part of my brain—the part that troubleshoots network latency and active directory syncs all day—that part tells me, "No, obviously there isn't a tiny person trapped in a box of old Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd records calling your name." I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I know how the world works. I know that voices don't just spontaneously generate from cardboard and vinyl in a dry room. 

But... but then there's the other part. The part of me that's actually lying there in the dark at 3:00 AM, when the white noise generator is off and the street is completely dead. And in those moments... God, it feels so real. It sounds as real as the hum of my refrigerator or the traffic out on the avenue during rush hour. It has texture, you know? Like, I can hear the breath behind the word. I can hear the slight distortion, like I mentioned, like a bad VoIP call where the packets are dropping just a little bit, but you can still make out exactly what the person is saying. And it's saying my name. It's not just random noise that my brain is trying to make sense of, like pareidolia for audio or whatever. It's specifically calling for me. 

So, do I believe it's real? In the daylight, sitting here in this office, looking out the window at the normal world? No, I know it's not real. I know it's some kind of glitch in my own hardware, a misfiring synapse or whatever. But when it's happening... when I'm standing there in my bare feet on the cold hardwood floor, staring at those moving boxes in the corner, and I hear that low, muffled voice... in that exact second, I believe it. I absolutely believe it's there. And that's what terrifies me, honestly. That I can know something is impossible, but still experience it as completely, undeniably real. It makes me question everything else, you know? Like, if my brain can fake that so perfectly, what else is it faking?
Do you think the voice you hear is trying to tell you something or send you a message?

Well, um... it doesn't say anything besides my name, so it's not like it's giving me instructions or, you know, reciting a manifesto or a warning or anything like that. But... it feels like an accusation. Like it’s trying to tell me that it *knows*. 

And that... that really messes with me, because it feeds right into this whole other thing that’s been happening to me during the day. It’s like this constant, heavy paranoia that I just can't shake, especially at work. I've been making these minor errors on my support tickets lately. Just stupid stuff, honestly, like miscategorizing a hardware request, or maybe taking too long to escalate a tier-2 network issue because I'm so tired, or forgetting to log my resolution notes before closing a ticket. 

My coworkers, they're great, and they keep telling me, "Hey man, don't worry about it, it's fine. Everyone messes up, those ticket errors are totally normal, especially with the new system update we just rolled out." They try to brush it off and tell me my metrics are still fine. But I just... I can't accept that. I get completely stuck on this idea—this absolute certainty, really—that the company is quietly tracking every single mistake I make. 

Like, I'm convinced there's a hidden dashboard somewhere, or some silent audit log that management and HR are reviewing every Friday afternoon behind closed doors. I just know they are building this massive, air-tight case to fire me. Because they’ve figured it out. They’ve figured out that I’m basically a fraud. That I don't actually know what I'm doing, that my degree is useless, and I've just been faking it this whole time. 

And I'll sit there at my desk, looking at the ticket queue, and every time an email pings from my supervisor, even if the subject line is just about a team lunch or a software patch, my stomach completely drops. Because my brain immediately goes, "This is it. This is the calendar invite for the meeting where they show you the logs, expose you, and walk you out of the building with your stuff in a cardboard box." 

So when I hear that voice at night, calling my name from the corner of the room... it just feels like an extension of that same feeling. Like the universe, or whatever is in those boxes, is just echoing what management already knows. That I'm a fake, and I'm caught, and my time is up. I just can't shake that belief, no matter how much logical evidence my team gives me that I'm doing fine. It's exhausting, honestly, just waiting for the axe to fall every single minute of the day.
Do you think the voice you hear is a part of your own mind or something outside of yourself?

Well, um... like I was saying before, about how it happens in this new, smaller apartment... when I hear that water dripping, or that low voice saying my name, it really doesn't feel like it's inside my head. It feels entirely outside of me. And I think about this a lot, because, you know, when I'm troubleshooting an audio issue on a user's machine at work, the first thing I do is isolate the source. Is it the internal speakers? Is it an external peripheral? Is there interference? 

So I try to apply that same diagnostic logic to myself. When I'm lying there, and the voice starts up, it has actual directional audio. It's not echoing inside my skull the way my own thoughts do, or the way a song gets stuck in your head. It is specifically originating from that boxed-up corner where my records are. If I turn my head on the pillow, the sound shifts in my ears, exactly the way a real, physical noise in the room would. 

That's why I always end up getting out of bed to check. Because it sounds so completely real at the time that my brain processes it as external audio data. I'll walk right up to those cardboard boxes, half expecting to find a speaker someone hid there as a prank, or a leak from the ceiling hitting the vinyl, but... there's nothing. Absolutely nothing there. 

So, logically, sitting here talking to you, I have to conclude that it’s a part of my own mind. It has to be, right? Because the physical evidence proves there is no external source. But it just... it doesn't *behave* like a thought. It behaves like a sound wave bouncing off the walls of my apartment. I've even caught myself thinking about bringing home a high-end condenser microphone from the AV department at work, just to record the room overnight. Just so I can look at the waveform on my monitor the next morning and have visual, hard data proving that the room was silent. Because my own senses are betraying me so thoroughly. It’s just so hard to accept that my own mind can fabricate something that feels so entirely outside of myself, right down to the acoustics of the room.
Do you think the voice you hear is trying to command you to do something specific?

No, no, it's... it's definitely not a command. Um, it never tells me to do anything. Like I was mentioning earlier about how this all happens in this new, smaller apartment I moved into... it's really just my name. Just that low voice saying my name from that boxed-up corner where my records are. 

And honestly, it's not even always a voice. Some nights, instead of the voice, I'll hear this very distinct sound of water dripping. Just... *drip... drip... drip*. Coming from that exact same corner. And my brain immediately goes into troubleshooting mode, right? I'm thinking, 'Great, a pipe is leaking behind the drywall, my vintage vinyl is going to get completely ruined, the landlord is going to try to pin the water damage on me.' 

So I get out of bed, I grab my phone, I turn on the flashlight app, and I go over to investigate. I'll check the ceiling, I'll feel the floorboards, I'll even pull the cardboard boxes away from the wall to look for water stains. And there's nothing. It's completely bone dry. But when I was lying there in the dark, it sounded completely real at the time. Both the dripping water and the voice... they sound so physically present in the room. But when I check, there's absolutely nothing there. 

So, to answer your question, no, it doesn't command me to do anything. It doesn't give me instructions or tell me to delete a server or anything crazy like that. It's just my name, or that dripping sound, and then just... nothing. I'll just stand there with my phone flashlight on, waiting for it to say something else, to give me a direction or finish the thought, but it never does.
Are you having trouble maintaining relationships with friends and family due to your current state?

Well, um... with friends, it's mostly... I have this group, we usually do these board-game nights, right? Like, heavy strategy games, stuff that takes a couple of hours to set up and play. But lately, I just... I've been skipping them. A lot of them, actually. I'll text them at the last minute and say I'm not feeling well, or I'm stuck on a late shift. And it's not that I don't want to see them, it's just that the thought of leaving the apartment, of having to sit there and pretend I'm fully present and keep track of all those rules and social interactions... it just feels overwhelmingly difficult. Keeping up with normal routines is just so much harder than it used to be. I barely leave the apartment anymore unless I absolutely have to. It just takes too much out of me. 

And, you know, it spills over into everything else, too, especially work. I am still working, thankfully, but... well, I mentioned those ticket errors earlier. It actually got to the point where I had to go to my supervisor—which, you know, absolutely terrified me because of that whole fear I have about them secretly building a case to fire me—but I had to ask for some accommodations. I asked if they could put an extra review process on my documentation for a little while. Because I'm just making these mistakes that I normally wouldn't make. I've been doing this for years, I know exactly how to document a server migration or a simple network protocol, but my brain just isn't holding onto the steps. 

So now I have a senior tech looking over my resolution logs before the tickets get completely closed out, just to be safe. It's embarrassing, honestly, having to ask for that kind of hand-holding at my age and with my experience, but I just don't have the bandwidth I used to. It's like I have to double-check every single thing I type, which just adds to the exhaustion, which makes me want to stay in my apartment even more. It's just this whole cycle where everything just feels so incredibly heavy to maintain.
Are you finding it harder to fulfill responsibilities at work or at home due to how you've been feeling?

Yeah, I mean... I think I actually kind of just touched on that a bit, with what I was saying about the board-game nights and the ticket errors. But to answer your question directly... yes. Absolutely yes. 

Like I was just mentioning, I am still working, which I'm grateful for, but the actual day-to-day responsibilities of the job have become a huge hurdle. Having to go and ask for those accommodations, getting a senior tech to do an extra review on my logs... I had to do that because I’m making documentation mistakes I normally wouldn’t ever make. And in IT support, documentation is basically the whole job, right? If you don't log the resolution steps accurately, the next tech who pulls a similar ticket is flying completely blind. So knowing I can't even trust myself to type up a basic summary without missing a critical step... it's incredibly frustrating. 

And then at home... well, I brought up how I skip some of those board-game nights now, and how I just leave the apartment a lot less in general. But it spills over into just the basic, mundane responsibilities, too. Keeping up with normal routines feels so much harder than it used to. I used to have a pretty strict system—you know, Sunday was always laundry and meal prep for the week, Tuesday was vacuuming, that sort of thing. Now, Sunday rolls around and I'll just sit on the couch for hours, staring at the wall, trying to mentally psych myself up just to put a load of darks in the washing machine. 

It’s like... if you think of it in tech terms, it’s like my brain's operating system is suddenly using 90% of its CPU just to keep the basic background processes running. There's almost zero processing power left for the actual applications—for doing my job, for seeing my friends, for keeping my apartment clean. So, yeah, whether it's at work or at home, just fulfilling those basic daily requirements takes so much more out of me than it ever did before.
Are you currently experiencing any hallucinations besides the voice you've mentioned?

Well, actually, I think I brought this up just a few minutes ago, but... no, not really anything besides what I already told you. I mean, there's the voice, and then there's that dripping water sound. I don't know if you'd classify the water as a hallucination, but since it's not actually happening, I guess it fits the bill, right? 

But yeah, I don't see things, I don't hear, you know, a choir singing or alarms going off or anything dramatic out of a movie. It's highly specific. It's just happening in this new, smaller apartment I moved into, and it's always, without fail, localized to that one corner where my records are still sitting in those cardboard boxes. It's either that low voice just saying my name, or some nights it's that very distinct *drip... drip... drip* of water. 

And like I was explaining before with the whole flashlight routine and checking for plumbing leaks, the craziest part is that it sounds completely real at the time. It has depth, it has volume, it sounds like the audio waves are physically bouncing off the walls and the boxes in the room. It triggers that immediate troubleshooting response in my head, like I have to go fix the hardware right then and there. But then I get out of bed, I go over, I pull the heavy boxes out, I check the drywall and the floorboards, and there is absolutely nothing there. It's bone dry and perfectly quiet. 

So, if you're asking if there are other things on top of that... no. Just the voice and the water, alternating, from that exact same corner. It's bizarre how my brain just generates those two specific audio files, so to speak, but no, nothing else besides those.
Do you hear the voice or the dripping sound every night, or does it come and go?

Well, it definitely comes and goes. It's not a constant, every-single-night kind of thing, which I guess is a small mercy, but... it's very tied to how I'm doing overall. 

Like, I never had those voices, or even that fixed fear I was telling you about—the one about being secretly watched at work and my supervisors building a case against me—I never experienced any of that before the move and before this whole... this heavy, dark feeling really set in. It's like they're a package deal, honestly. They only really show up on the same bad stretches when I'm feeling incredibly low, you know? When the guilt is just eating at me because I'm ignoring my friends or messing up my tickets, and I'm just completely worn down to the bone. When I hit that point of total emotional and physical exhaustion, that's when the voice starts saying my name, or the dripping starts up in the corner of the room. 

But on the days when I'm actually doing okay—when I have a little bit of energy and the weight lifts just a fraction, and I can actually focus a bit better—the apartment is totally quiet. No dripping, no voice, and that intense fear at work kind of fades into the background. 

It's almost like a system error that only triggers when my internal CPU is completely maxed out and overheating. If I have any bandwidth left, if I'm doing alright, it doesn't happen. The hardware runs fine. But the second I'm drained and feeling low and guilty again, it's like my mental firewall just drops, and all those weird glitches and fears just come right back online. So, yeah, it fluctuates completely based on how bad the rest of it is getting.
Are you currently experiencing any hallucinations besides the voice and the dripping water sound?

I... wait, didn't you just ask me that? Like, literally two questions ago? I'm pretty sure I just went over this whole thing with you. But, I mean, I can explain it again if you need me to clarify something. 

Like I was saying before, the answer is no. I'm not experiencing any other hallucinations. It's just the two things I've already detailed for you. It's the voice and the water. And it's highly specific. It only happens on some nights, and it only happens in this new, smaller apartment I moved into. I never had anything like this happen at my old place, which was a lot bigger and had better soundproofing, but here, it's very localized. 

It always comes from that one specific corner in the living room area where I've got all my vinyl records stacked up in those heavy U-Haul cardboard boxes. I haven't unpacked them yet because, well, I just haven't had the energy, like I mentioned earlier with the laundry and everything else. So they're just sitting there, taking up space. And from that exact corner, I'll either hear this low voice—just a single voice, very deep, saying my first name—or I'll hear this incredibly distinct dripping sound. *Drip... drip... drip.* Like a leaky pipe or a faucet that isn't closed all the way. 

And I know I already told you this, but the part that really messes with my head is how completely, 100% real it sounds in the moment. It doesn't sound like a thought in my head; it sounds like external audio. It has spatial awareness, if that makes sense. Like my ears are picking up actual sound waves bouncing off the cardboard boxes. That's why I end up doing that whole troubleshooting routine I told you about, getting out of bed, grabbing my phone flashlight, moving the heavy boxes around to check the baseboards and the drywall for water damage. Because my brain is telling me, 'Hey, there is a physical problem with the plumbing in this corner, you need to fix it before it ruins your records.' 

But then I check, and... nothing. It's totally dry. There's no water, there's no person standing there saying my name. It's just empty space and boxes. So, yeah, I know I'm repeating myself here, but to answer your question again... no, there is absolutely nothing else besides the low voice and the dripping water in that one corner of the apartment. Just those two specific things.
Do you feel like you're a burden to others most of the day?

A burden? Yeah. I mean, honestly, that’s a huge part of what actually brought me in here to see you in the first place. It’s just this constant, heavy feeling that I absolutely cannot shake, no matter what I do. It’s this deep-seated sense that I’ve just... ruined things for everyone. 

Take my job, for example. I’m a support specialist, so my entire role is literally supposed to be helping people, fixing their hardware issues, keeping things running smoothly. But because I’ve been falling so far behind at work lately, I’m just creating more problems. Every time I miss an SLA or have to pass off a basic ticket to one of my coworkers because I just don’t have the mental bandwidth to troubleshoot it, I know I’m making their day harder. I’m actively dragging the rest of the team down. 

And then you combine that with losing total control of the apartment situation—which, I know I keep bringing up the apartment and the boxes and everything, but it’s all connected.
